description: Finally after all of this time I finally got one of these to share with you. These guys are one of the most common feeder birds and they are one of the most familiar looking song birds to many of us bird nerds and enthusiasts. You may notice these guys feeding in a guild with chickadees, wrens, Kinglets, and other small birds some birds it is seen with are only seen in winter. The Tufted Titmouse is found in the eastern portion of the United States. These birds are small grey, with a white breast and a black square on the forehead. They feed on safflower when at feeders but feed one other things when out in the wild. They prefer to eat safflower but also been known to feed on peanuts and I have seen a couple go for suet at my feeder station. The Tufted Titmouse is related to the Chickadees or the Tit family. These guys make a verity of calls. They make a rattling call when threatened, a loudly whistled "Peter Peter Peter" sound. They have a really cool crest and sometimes when it is down it may look funny to some beginners. They normally have it raised when excited or threatened. They absolutely hate birds of prey; or anything that looks like one. I have been a couple of places where we had stuffed and mounted taxidermy Owls for educational programs where droves of the birds saw them and start chattering their alarm calls. These guys don't like anything that resembles owls or raptors. I had this happen on a night hike at Pinnacle Mountain State Park in Arkansas, and one time when I was Volunteering at River Legacy Living Science Center during the Great Backyard Bird Count. These birds are ones you are most likely to encounter somewhere along your everyday travels to the woods. They are quite common and a favorite of a lot of birders. These guys are very fidgety and very hard to photograph sometimes. I have trouble getting them sometimes along with the Carolina Chickadees.

description:
The photo was taken at 10:13 a.m. on Lettuce Park. The temperature at that time was 87 degrees Fahrenheit with a humidity level of forty-eight percent. The specimen I encountered was having a nice meal on a birdfeeder; it perched humbly upon the wooden stool along with other members of its class. The specimen had a grey coat and a long tail matching his ebony eyes. 

What made me believe this was a Northern Mockingbird was its overall physicality as both species have grey feathers and are found year-long on the south. The beak of the bird also had a hint of a downward beak (better appreciated in the second photo). They also tend to be more roundish birds although that could easily be explained by the mockingbird having a nice meal. 

I found the iNaturalist suggestions to be the most helpful when helping me determine the species, as well as the website: 
https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Mockingbird/id

description:
The Tufted Titmouse is scientifically recognized as Baeolophus bicolor. It is in close relation to chickadees. The Tufted Titmouse size is typically 5 to 6 inches in length. 
Its color is a blue-silvery grey with a white belly, some soft orange tinges around the wings and a black patch on top of its bill. It is typically found in forests of eastern states. it has an affinity for very tall trees and forested areas. This species was actually found in an cool open area within a city park with tall trees and bird feeders. Its population is expanding to more northern states as temperatures rise.

Additional information can be found at

description: This bird was identified as a Tufted titmouse because of its gray coloring and the pointed crest on top of its head. It was darker in color on the edges of its wings and had a black spot just above its beak. It also had a white abdomen with some light brown coloration on its sides. Tufted titmice are secondary consumers. This species tends to have 1-2 broods per year and typically breeds during the spring. Females lay 3-9 eggs that hatch after about two weeks. The young birds are considered sexually mature adults after about a year. This bird was likely an adult, as juveniles lack the black spot on their foreheads. The sex could not be determined as this species does not exhibit any noticeable sexual dimorphism. Tufted titmice can be found in habitats such as forests, swamps, and suburban areas. Other organisms that may also live in these habitats include woody and herbaceous plants, insects, squirrels, and frogs. This bird was found on a bird feeder in a suburban area. A potential predator of this species is Cooper’s hawk (Accipiter cooperii) and a potential source of prey are berries like those of the American Holly (Ilex opaca). A potential competitor of this species is the Black-capped chickadee (Poecile atricapillus).

description: Tufted Titmouse’s are secondary consumer, eating primarily insects in the wormer months. They are a small, grey bird with large black eyes. As the name suggests, the tufted titmouse has a “tuft” or small crest on its head, providing a soft point to the silhouette. They can be slightly lighter in color on their bellies, with a typically coloring being a light brown or beige on the underside and grey on the back of it. They can also have other slight color details, such as a reddish patch, or some white around the tail feathers. They do not often gather in large groups beyond their breeding season, which can be helpful for identifying them. Tufted Titmice typically lay clutched of around 5-8 eggs. Once these babies hatch, they may stay with the parents until they reach a juvenal stage, at which point the will likely leave. In rare cases, the juvenile titmouse may say with the parents for more than a year. The tufted titmouse I saw was an adult, I was not able to sex it. These birds occur in forested habitats, and often thrive in suburbs or other areas with bird feeders, as they are frequent visitors. One predator of the tufted titmouse is the raccoon, which eats the eggs. Prey for the titmouse include horse flies, and a competitor is the blue jay, which compete for nesting space.

description: Seemingly high up in one of the trees surrounding the stormwater ponds. About an hour before sunset.

Date: March 6th, 2021
Time: 9:10 - 10:37
Location: Centennial Woods
Habitat: Urban forest patch
Weather: Partly cloudy, 9 mph W.
Temperature: -8 C
Species Number: 10
Total Individuals: 56
Species List: x8 Red Crossbill (Type 10), x7 American Robin, x1 Downy Woodpecker, x15 Black-capped Chickadee, x1 Dark-eyed Junco, x2 Northern Cardinal, x19 Rock Pigeon, x1 Red-breasted Nuthatch, x1 Tufted Titmouse, x1 American Crow. 

Field Journal Three
	I was surprised to see and hear so many birds on our trip through Centennial Woods. I assumed that most birds were migratory and just left for more hospitable temperatures. This is not necessarily the case though, as the major reason for migration is actually access to food! The snow covers up much of the ground and bushes that might have seeds, nuts, berries or insects on them. So how do these birds deal? 
	For starters, they might find a good place to cozy up. Woodpeckers leave many holes in trees by drilling for insects to eat. These holes can also provide a good nook to rest in and conserve heat and energy. Birds that nest in these are called cavity nesters. The smaller holes may even provide a home for a bird like the White-breasted Nuthatch or a Chickadee. Finding a hole with the perfect fit is essential in minimizing the amount of cold wind and snow the bird is exposed to. Birds like the Northern Cardinal will also fluff their feathers to increase insulation. The extra air trapped between their feathers helps put up a barrier against the cold. 
A bird’s diet is likely to change a lot in the winter. As most of the ground is covered, alternative food sources must be considered. Seeds dropped by trees, saps, or even carrion become more common as the tasty insects die in the cold. Another example, the highbush cranberry is a very bitter berry bush that is not usually consumed by birds. However, if there are not other options, this bitter berry might seem much more appealing. 

Dead Snag Activity
	I saw fifty-three snags over the course of two trips through Centennial Woods. The first of which were recorded Saturday during the field trip with the second of which were recorded Sunday along a different route. The most common snags left standing seemed to be larger conifers such as white pine. Most dead snags had one to three larger cavities in them, while living or partially dead trees had smaller and more abundant cavities. In one example we passed, a huge white pine had been riddled with small holes about the size of a pinky finger. This tree was still alive, but the dead deciduous tree next to it had far fewer holes, and were much larger. The size differences may be related to food sources; where the living tree has tons of bugs hiding in bark, the dead tree may not have as many bugs to hunt. The wood of a dead tree may be easier to drill into and better fit for cavity nesting than a tough living tree. Given how many I found, it may be that certain patches of trees are better for cavity nesters than others. The conifers generally provide much more cover in the winter, and these areas of forest could be more abundant with birds than a more deciduous patch. Snags are important in maintaining a prosperous environment, not just food and shelter for birds. After a snag falls, it becomes a nurse log that provides resources for ground dwelling bugs, mosses, and fungi! As it is further broken down the tree feeds the growth of the rest of the forest.

description:
Description: This species was found in Lettuce Lake Park in the late afternoon. It was 68° and sunny. This species kept flying up the trees and back to the ground. It is a small songbird. It has a gray body with a white undertone and orange/brown sides. Additionally, it has a pointed crest on its head. It’s lifespan is 2.1 years old and it can be 5-7 inches long with a 9-11 inch wingspan (UMich). The appear in various colors and sizes. They can be found within dense tree species. They prefer temperate habitats within deciduous woodlands similar to where the species was observed (Cornell University). They are found within the southeastern side of the United States. They eat insects, nuts, and berries. Their behavior includes flying from branch to branch and hanging on various branches in search of food (Cornell University). They open seeds with their beaks and build nests using leaves, moss, and bark. It takes 1-2 weeks to build their nests (Cornell). They reproduce during breeding season (March and May) by other birds and their eggs lay in the nests 3-90 feet above the ground (UMich). Some have multiple broods each season. They are active birds and they communicate with each other with call sounds (UMich). They help control insect populations. 

Cornell University. Tufted Titmouse. 2016. https://celebrateurbanbirds.org/learn/birds/focal-species/tufted-titmouse/#:~:text=Habitat,at%20elevations%20above%202%2C000%20feet.
